title: Visit the graves
hookLine: the Prophet encouraged visiting graves, for they remind of death and the hereafter (Sahih Muslim)

lines: A MAN AT HIS MOTHER'S GRAVE.
cards: A grave, and a grown man standing at it, crying. It's his mother's grave, and he has come to see where she lies. The people with him start crying too, because he is.
The man is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the scene is in Sahih Muslim, a collection of reports of his words and deeds.
When he speaks, he ends with advice for everyone standing there, and for anyone who has ever avoided a cemetery.

teach.b: In another report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says something surprising: I had forbidden you to visit graves, but now visit them.
A rule was set, then lifted, and the report keeps both halves, the old no and the new yes, in a single sentence.

At his mother's grave, he gives the reason plainly: visit the graves, for they remind you of death. Reports in other collections add that they remind you of the hereafter. The point isn't to stay sad.
A grave is a teacher. It doesn't lecture. It just stands there with a name on it, saying: this happens to everyone, and then comes what comes next.
The hadith don't picture walking into a cemetery in silence.
Reports in the same collection describe a greeting to the people in the graves: peace be upon you, dwellers of these homes, believers; and we, God willing, will join you.
The dead are spoken to as neighbors. It's easy to arrange a life that never passes a grave; in some towns, cemeteries sit at the edge, behind walls.
This hadith turns that around: go on purpose, so the living remember they are on the same road.
In Muslim teaching, the visit is a kindness to the dead, with prayers for them, and to the living, a reminder while there's still time to use it.

how: Muslims visit graves, in some communities on Fridays or around the Eids, greeting the dead with a salam, reciting Quran and praying for mercy for them; practices such as praying to the dead or wailing at graves are discouraged.

games.q: what's inside the visit — tap the pairs.

s: an early ban was lifted: now visit them.
the Prophet visited his mother's grave and wept
and those with him wept too.
the hadith picture entering a cemetery in silence
hadith describe a greeting of peace to the people of the graves.

games.q: you're at a cemetery for the first time in years. what does the hadith suggest you do as you enter?
games.why: peace be upon you, dwellers of these homes; and we, God willing, will join you.

practice: Bring to mind a grave you know, a grandparent's, a friend's, a stranger's you once walked past, or a place where someone's ashes rest, and stand there in your mind, seeing the ground, the stone, the name.
Let it remind you of what it reminds you of, without pushing. If you pray, you can greet the dead there, or ask mercy for them, in words you already know.

wordCard.voice: Sahih Muslim, the hadith collection where the Prophet, having once forbidden it, now tells people to visit graves, because they remind the living of death. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: they remind us. A grave teaches without saying a word. Day seven hundred eighty-five, done.

sources.ref: Sunan Ibn Majah 1569 (graves remind of the hereafter)
